# Transmission won't go into gear - Strange

When you swap a 1.8L engine for a 2.0L JDM unit in a 2000 Mazda Protege, the drivetrain dynamics change subtly but significantly. Your new engine is idling smoothly and revving fine, which rules out a complete mechanical failure of the powertrain itself. However, the symptom you are describingâwhere the automatic transmission only engages after revving to 2500â3000 RPMâis a classic indicator of hydraulic pressure issues or solenoid logic problems. Since you did not pull the transmission and left all electrical connections intact, the issue is almost certainly related to fluid levels or air in the system rather than internal mechanical destruction.

The most critical clue lies in your fluid check. You noted that with the engine hot and running, the fluid level was already higher than the MAX mark on the dipstick. This is a red flag for an automatic transmission. Unlike many manual transmissions where "hot" levels are forgiving, automatic transmissions rely on precise hydraulic pressure to move clutch packs and bands. If the fluid is overfilled, even slightly, it can cause the fluid to aerate (turn into foam) due to the agitation of the pump.

Foamy fluid acts like a compressible gas rather than an incompressible liquid. When you attempt to shift gears, the transmission control module (TCM) or internal valve body expects immediate pressure buildup. If the fluid is foamy, that pressure cannot be generated quickly enough. This explains why the car only engages when revved high: increasing RPM increases pump speed, which forces fluid through the system faster than the foam can collapse, momentarily building enough pressure to lock up the clutch packs.

Adding another half quart of fluid to an already overfilled pan worsened the situation immediately. You confirmed that after topping it off, the transmission would not engage in any gear, even with high RPM. This confirms the diagnosis: the system is now flooded with air-entrained fluid. The solution is straightforward but requires patience. You must drain the excess fluid to bring the level down to the "Full" or "Hot" range indicated on the dipstick, typically 1/2 inch above the cross-hatch mark when the engine is running and warmed up.

Once you have corrected the fluid level, you will likely need to perform a fluid exchange cycle. Simply topping off might leave residual air bubbles trapped in the valve body or torque converter. Running the vehicle through all gears while gently bumping them can help purge the air, but be prepared for the transmission to slip or fail to engage until the last few shifts are completed.

A common pitfall with dipsticks is reading them when the fluid is cold. If you checked the level before the engine reached operating temperature, the volume of fluid would be lower due to thermal contraction. However, since your initial check showed "higher than MAX" while hot, and adding more fluid made it worse, the error was almost certainly in the initial fill volume or a slight leak from the radiator cooler that wasn't fully accounted for during the refill.

In the context of modern automotive maintenance, this scenario highlights why following manufacturer specifications for fluid capacity is non-negotiable. Overfilling an automatic transmission is one of the few mistakes that can turn a healthy unit into a slipping mess within minutes. If the issue persists after draining to the correct level and bleeding the system, you may need to inspect the radiator cooler line seals or check for air pockets in the filter screen if your Protege utilizes one.
